[LLM] Defender exclusion added via Add-MpPreference for campaign install path Installation Medium
Detects the defense-evasion step where the malware runs PowerShell with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to call Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath, carving out its hidden D3F4E2A1 install location from Microsoft Defender scanning. Flags the exclusion-add behaviour, prioritising command lines that reference the campaign's Caches\D3F4E2A1 path. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim PowerShell evasion command (Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass) and boosts confidence when the exclusion path references the D3F4E2A1 / Caches install location. Kept as hunting because legit admins occasionally add exclusions. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = CommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: Run key WinSysCache Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's machine/user Run-key persistence value named WinSysCache under CurrentVersion\Run, which re-launches the hidden RuntimeHost.exe miner/loader at logon. The value name is a campaign-specific masquerade for 'Windows System Cache'. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Run-key value name WinSysCache under both HKLM and HKCU CurrentVersion\Run — a unique masquerade string that legitimate software does not use, making the registry-value name alone high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1547.001

| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "WinSysCache"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "WinSysCache"

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: 'Windows System Health' scheduled tasks Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's masqueraded scheduled tasks — 'Windows System Health' (logon), 'Windows System Health Monitor' (boot +1h), and 'Windows System Health Check' (every 5 min) — all running with highest privileges to relaunch the miner/loader. These exact task names are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the three verbatim task names from the article's persistence table ('Windows System Health', '... Monitor', '... Check'); these names plus highest-privilege triggers are unique to the campaign and don't match any genuine Windows task. Defender query covers both schtasks.exe execution and the ScheduledTaskCreated telemetry for API-created tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
  | where AdditionalFields has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=AdditionalFields
)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698
| where EventData has "Windows System Health"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where DvcAction != "Block"

            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

status: experimental

author: Clankerusecase

    category: process_creation

            - '\outlook.exe'

            - '\mspub.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/

author: Clankerusecase

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] KnowledgeDeliver ViewState deserialization RCE: w3wp.exe spawns OS shells (CVE-2026-5426) Exploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment of CVE-2026-5426 where a malicious signed ViewState payload achieves OS-level code execution and the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawns command interpreters or recon binaries. This is the highest-fidelity signal of the KnowledgeDeliver zero-day chain and the Godzilla web shell command execution. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact post-exploitation behaviour — ViewState deserialization yields OS-level RCE under the IIS worker w3wp.exe. The w3wp.exe parent + shell/recon child pair is called out explicitly as a strong signal by Mandiant/Google Cloud and Rescana write-ups of CVE-2026-5426. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/85088/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","tasklist.exe","reg.exe","schtasks.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\tasklist.exe","\\reg.exe","\\schtasks.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS Worker Process Spawning Command Interpreter (KnowledgeDeliver ViewState RCE)
id: 5f3c1a82-9d44-4e21-b1aa-2c9f0e7d4b10
description: Detects w3wp.exe spawning command shells or recon binaries, indicative of ViewState deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-5426) and Godzilla web shell command execution.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/knowledgedeliver-flaw-exploited-as-a-zero-day-to-install-web-shells/
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\w3wp.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\whoami.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
      - '\nltest.exe'
      - '\systeminfo.exe'
      - '\ipconfig.exe'
      - '\tasklist.exe'
      - '\reg.exe'
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\reg.exe OR *\\schtasks.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/w3wp\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|net|net1|nltest|systeminfo|ipconfig|tasklist|reg|schtasks|certutil|bitsadmin|rundll32|cscript|wscript)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","tasklist.exe","reg.exe","schtasks.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
[LLM] ASP.NET ViewState MAC verification failures (Event ID 1316) on KnowledgeDeliver IIS hosts Exploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation-attempt fingerprint of CVE-2026-5426: ASP.NET logging ViewState MAC validation failures (Application log Event ID 1316, source ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0, event code 4009). Repeated or first-seen failures on an internet-facing IIS host indicate an actor trialing crafted/signed ViewState payloads against the shared hardcoded machineKey. Rationale: Event ID 1316 / ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0 code 4009 ("Viewstate verification failed") is explicitly named by corroborating analyses of this campaign as the canonical exploit-attempt signal. Defender Advanced Hunting has no Application-channel table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; Datadog/Falcon also do not list the Application channel, hence empty. Threshold (>=3) is empirical to cut benign single-event post-deploy noise. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where EventID == 1316
| where Source startswith "ASP.NET"
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("Viewstate","MAC validation","4009")
| summarize Failures = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(RenderedDescription) by Computer
| where Failures >= 3
| order by Failures desc

[LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing .aspx/.js/.config — Godzilla web shell drop & malicious JS injection Installation Medium
Hunts the install/persistence step of the KnowledgeDeliver intrusion where the compromised IIS worker writes web-servable files: dropping the Godzilla (.NET) web shell as .aspx, or modifying an application JavaScript file to prompt users to install a fake 'security authentication plugin' and load an attacker-controlled script. Targets file-write telemetry attributed to w3wp.exe. Rationale: Directly models the article's two install actions — Godzilla deployed as a .NET web shell and an application JavaScript file modified to load an attacker script / fake plugin. Attribution of the write to w3wp.exe is the high-fidelity constraint; benign apps rarely have the worker process write .aspx/.js to web roots at runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or SHA1 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2") or MD5 in~ ("7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Risky/anonymized Microsoft Entra sign-in to Salesforce resource (ShinyHunters vishing ATO) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Unauthorized Salesforce connected-app (malicious Data Loader) authorization
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Salesforce bulk/mass data export burst from anonymized IP (UNC6040 exfiltration) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Risky/anonymized Microsoft Entra sign-in to Salesforce resource (ShinyHunters vishing ATO) Delivery Medium
Hunts the Charter initial-access step: a vishing-compromised Microsoft Entra account producing a successful interactive sign-in flagged risky or from anonymizing/VPN infrastructure (UNC6040 favours Mullvad VPN) where the target resource is Salesforce. Ties the SSO compromise to the specific SaaS app the actor exfiltrated from. Rationale: Article states Charter's Entra account was vished and used to export from Salesforce; pivots on the Salesforce resource (ResourceDisplayName/appDisplayName) plus risk/anonymizer flags rather than a generic risky-login, matching UNC6040's Mullvad-VPN access pattern (cross-checked Google TI and MITRE C0059). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0059/

[LLM] Unauthorized Salesforce connected-app (malicious Data Loader) authorization Installation Medium
Hunts UNC6040's signature step: during the vishing call the actor walks the victim to the Salesforce connected-app setup page to authorize a malicious/modified 'Data Loader' OAuth app. Surfaces new connected-app authorizations in the Salesforce tenant via Defender for Cloud Apps, especially from anonymized infrastructure. Rationale: Article describes ShinyHunters breaching Salesforce via abused OAuth/connected-app access; the malicious 'Data Loader' connected-app authorization is the documented UNC6040 hallmark (Google TI), so matching on the app name + OAuth authorization action is high-fidelity. Sentinel left empty: Salesforce connected-app authorizations do not surface in the canonical Entra AuditLogs/SigninLogs tables; Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as Salesforce SaaS telemetry is not shipped to those sources in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6040-proactive-hardening-recommendations

[LLM] Salesforce bulk/mass data export burst from anonymized IP (UNC6040 exfiltration) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Charter exfiltration step: millions of customer records pulled from Salesforce via Bulk API / report exports in a short burst. Counts export-style activities per account/window in Defender for Cloud Apps and prioritizes those originating from anonymizing/VPN infrastructure characteristic of UNC6040. Rationale: Article quotes 40M records exfiltrated from Salesforce; UNC6040 exfil is documented as REST pagination / Bulk API download bursts (Google TI). Thresholded burst-count on export actions per account is the correct shape (not a single-event Sigma). Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: Salesforce export telemetry is only available here via Defender for Cloud Apps, not those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/voice-phishing-data-extortion • https://attack.mitre.org/campaigns/C0059/
ATT&CKT1213 T1119
Data sources
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where ActionType has_any ("Export","ReportExport","MassDownload","BulkApi","Download","QueryAll")
| where AccountDisplayName !endswith "$"
| summarize ExportEvents = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            AnyAnon = max(tostring(IsAnonymousProxy)),
            SampleAction = any(ActionType),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ISPs = make_set(ISP, 10)
            by AccountDisplayName, AccountId, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where ExportEvents > 50    // 50 export ops / 10 min = bulk-pull burst, well above interactive baseline
| order by ExportEvents desc
APPLICATION
index=salesforce (EVENT_TYPE="BulkApi" OR EVENT_TYPE="ReportExport" OR EVENT_TYPE="RestApi" OR action="MassDownload") | bin _time span=10m | stats sum(ROW_COUNT) as rows dc(EVENT_TYPE) as evtypes values(SOURCE_IP) as src by USER_NAME, _time | where rows > 100000 | sort - rows
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] XWiki unauthenticated XAR import via REST POST /rest/wikis/{wikiName} (CVE-2026-33137) Exploitation High
Hunts successful, unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the XWiki REST XAR-import endpoint (/xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/]) that return 2xx, which is exactly the exploitation primitive in CVE-2026-33137 — the import runs with no auth/authz check, letting an attacker create or update wiki documents. The Authorization-header-absent + 2xx-status combination separates exploitation from legitimate authenticated XAR imports performed by admins/migration tooling. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's exact exploitation primitive — POST to /wikis/{wikiName} performing a XAR import with no auth check. Confirmed via XWiki docs/dev list that the real path is /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName} (POST, optional ?backup=&history= params, XAR in body), so the regex on /rest/wikis/<single-segment> plus 2xx plus absent Authorization header is high-fidelity for unauthenticated exploitation vs legitimate authenticated imports. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrvh-r3f2-9h4r • https://jira.xwiki.org/browse/XWIKI-23953 • https://www.xwiki.org/xwiki/bin/view/Documentation/UserGuide/Features/XWikiRESTfulAPI • https://devs.xwiki.narkive.com/KEuNSQkQ/xwiki-vote-add-rest-api-to-import-a-xar-file
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/rest/wikis/[^/?#]+/?($|\?)"   // /xwiki/rest/wikis/{wikiName}[/] XAR-import endpoint
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","202")            // import accepted/succeeded
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)              // CVE-2026-33137: import runs with NO auth header
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MuddyWater Uses DLL Side-Loading in Espionage Campaign Targeting 9 Countries

The Hacker News
2026-05-26 17 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Iranian hacking group known as MuddyWater has been linked to a new campaign affecting at least nine organizations across nine countries on four continents in the first quarter of 2026. The activity targeted industrial and electronics manufacturing, education and public-sector bodies, financial services, and professional services, per the Threat Hunter Team from Symantec and Carbon Black.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — MuddyWater Uses DLL Side-Loading in Espionage Campaign Targeting 9 Countries
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll · [LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading rogue fmapp.dll Installation High
Hunts the legitimately-signed Fortemedia audio binary fmapp.exe side-loading a malicious fmapp.dll (Operation Olalampo lineage) from a non-standard directory. The rogue DLL embeds ChromElevator and beacons to attacker IP 157.20.182.49, so a fmapp.exe running outside its Program Files install path is the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Uses the article's exact loader/DLL pair (fmapp.exe→fmapp.dll) plus the non-standard-path heuristic that separates the MuddyWater drop from legitimate Fortemedia audio software; pair documented by Group-IB (Operation Olalampo) and confirmed by Symantec. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/ • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "fmapp.exe"
| where FileName =~ "fmapp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ModulePath = FolderPath, ModuleSHA256 = SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel has no native image-load table; pivot on process execution of the signed loader from a non-standard path
let legitPaths = dynamic(["C:\\Program Files","C:\\Program Files (x86)","C:\\Windows"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\fmapp.exe"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any (legitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater DLL side-load: SentinelOne sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading rogue sentinelagentcore.dll Installation High
Hunts deliberate abuse of the signed SentinelOne binary sentinelmemoryscanner.exe to side-load a rogue sentinelagentcore.dll — chosen by MuddyWater specifically to evade signature-based detection. The rogue DLL name and any execution outside the SentinelOne install path is the discriminator. Rationale: sentinelmemoryscanner.exe → sentinelagentcore.dll is an exact named pair from the article; the rogue DLL name plus execution outside the SentinelOne directory makes this near-zero-FP, and Symantec/GBHackers confirm the deliberate security-product binary abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://gbhackers.com/seedworm-apt-abuses-signed-binaries/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

[LLM] MuddyWater node.exe implant chain spawning PowerShell recon Exploitation High
Hunts the MuddyWater node.exe-based implant chain that drops and launches PowerShell to perform reconnaissance, screenshot capture, SAM hive theft, privilege escalation and SOCKS5 reverse-proxy tunnelling. A node.exe parent spawning powershell.exe/cmd.exe is highly atypical of benign Node.js application behaviour. Rationale: Targets the article's specific node.exe→PowerShell implant chain (the unusual JS-runtime-as-loader pivot) rather than generic PowerShell; Symantec and BleepingComputer both describe node.exe dropping PowerShell recon scripts including SAM theft and SOCKS5 tunnelling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

[LLM] SAM/SYSTEM hive theft via reg.exe save under MuddyWater node/PowerShell chain Actions on Objectives High
Hunts registry-hive export of the SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY hives via reg.exe save or PowerShell, used by the MuddyWater PowerShell scripts to harvest local credentials for lateral movement. Scoped to a node.exe/PowerShell parent lineage to keep it article-specific. Rationale: Implements the article's 'SAM hive theft' step with the canonical reg.exe save HKLM\SAM pattern (plus SYSTEM/SECURITY needed to decrypt it); machine-account exclusion and hive-name scoping keep FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] MuddyWater C2 beacon to 157.20.182.49 and campaign domains Command & Control High
Alerts on outbound connections to the MuddyWater C2 IP 157.20.182.49 (the address the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to) and the campaign domains timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com. Elevated confidence when the initiating process is one of the side-load loaders or node.exe. Rationale: 157.20.182.49 is the attacker IP the side-loaded fmapp.dll connects to (attributed by Huntress in the article); timetrakr.cloud and svc.wompworthy.com are pre-extracted campaign domains. IP/domain matches are inherently high-fidelity—validate the IP against threat-intel before broad alerting as only the article/Huntress cite it. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/iran-seedworm-electronics

[LLM] MuddyWater data exfiltration staging to sendit.sh file-transfer service Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts upload/staging of stolen data to the public file-transfer service sendit.sh, used by MuddyWater to exfiltrate collected data. Detects DNS/web connections to sendit.sh, especially from non-browser processes such as PowerShell, node.exe or curl. Rationale: sendit.sh is the specific public file-transfer service the article names as the data-staging destination; restricting to non-browser initiators (PowerShell/node/curl) separates exfil tooling from incidental user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/muddywater-uses-dll-side-loading-in.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/iranian-hackers-targeted-major-south-korean-electronics-maker/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667", "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc", "b21c802775df0c0d82c8cfde299084abc624898b10258db641b820172a0ba29a", "589ecb0bb31adc6101b9e545a4e5e07ae2e97d464b0a62242a498e613a7740b6"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc
